LLM survey personas

Project scope

Four deliverables were defined from the brief. Working constraints: approximately six hours total work.

DeliverableOutput
100 LLM-based personasOne saved representation per respondent, fitted from known answers.
Single-select surveyFive new questions, answer probabilities and 500 sampled responses.
Method comparisonThree approaches reviewed; one implemented and evaluated.
FindingsHuman-answer comparisons, baseline results, limitations and next steps.

Work sequence

  • Data: select a dataset and related decision; preserve question wording; define splits.
  • Modelling: encode questions and options; train the shared scorer; fit respondent vectors.
  • Evaluation: compare individual answers and group shares; test the contribution of respondent vectors.
  • Simulation: ask five new questions and report the resulting support estimates.

Dataset and decision

2,058U.S. survey respondents
4linked survey waves
100held-out people to model
  • Dataset: Twin-2K-500, with linked demographic, environmental, economic and policy responses.
  • Selection rationale: known and held-out answers are available for the same respondents.
  • Target group: 100 held-out members of a historical U.S. Prolific panel; no population weighting.

Dataset: Toubia et al., Twin-2K-500 (2025).

Policy question

How should a hypothetical $1 billion budget be allocated between immediate energy-bill credits and home energy improvements?

  • Relevant evidence: environmental attitudes, economic preferences and related policy opinions.
  • Fixed conditions: total budget and low-income eligibility. Variable: allocation between the two forms of support.
  • Intended use: identify allocations for human testing. Programme effectiveness was not assessed.

Methods considered

Three construction approaches were reviewed. The frozen-encoder approach was implemented; the other two were not experimentally benchmarked.

01

Evidence-grounded prompting

  • Survey history or interviews supplied as context to a generative LLM.
  • Low setup cost; predictions depend on evidence selection and prompting.

Park et al., self-report grounded agents (2026 revision)

02

Survey fine-tuning

  • Language-model weights or adapters trained on human survey responses.
  • Additional training and validation requirements. SubPOP evaluates subpopulation distributions, a different target from individual twins.

Suh et al., SubPOP (ACL 2025); Hu et al., LoRA (2021)

03

Frozen encoder and learned response model (implemented)

  • Frozen Qwen features combined with a shared scorer and an eight-number vector per respondent.
  • Selected for low training cost, inspectable parameters and straightforward baseline comparisons.
  • Main limitation: semantic features may miss distinctions that affect human answers.

Encoder: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B model card

Data splits and evaluation

GroupPermitted evidencePurpose
1,658 background people430 training questionsFit the feature reduction, shared scoring model and background person vectors.
300 development people92 anchor questions per personFit their vectors; compare candidates on eight validation questions.
100 final people92 anchor questions per personFit the final personas; evaluate on three reserved policy questions, then simulate five new ones.
  • Anchors: known answers used to fit each respondent vector.
  • Leakage controls: held-out question answers excluded across all people and waves; full-persona summaries excluded.
  • Checks: original wording, option mappings, missing responses and embedding retrieval verified. Split seed: 20261023.
  • Model selection: seven variants compared in two rounds using eight validation items: two policy and six maximisation questions.
  • Final test: predictions saved before labels were opened; no subsequent model changes. Three related policy items, not a whole-survey holdout.

Reserved topics: carbon-emissions tax; 40% of new clean-energy infrastructure development spending directed to low-income communities; federal investment in carbon-pollution-free electricity by 2035.

Evaluation metrics

Exact-answer accuracy
How often the highest-probability option matches the human’s selected option.
Log loss
How much probability the model assigns to the observed answer. Lower is better.
Group error
How far predicted answer shares or support shares are from the observed group. Lower is better.

Model architecture

1. Shared model training

  • Input per candidate: scenario, question, all options and candidate answer.
  • Frozen Qwen: 1,024 features. Training-fitted PCA: 64 features.
  • Shared scorer and background respondent vectors trained jointly on 712,827 observed responses.

2. Persona fitting

  • Shared weights fixed; eight coordinates fitted per final respondent from 92 permitted anchors.
  • 100 saved vectors fitted from 9,198 observed answers; two missing answers excluded.

3. Response prediction

  • Question-answer features and the saved respondent vector produce option scores; softmax gives probabilities.
  • Individual response: one sampled option. Group estimate: average probabilities across personas.

Response model

score(i, q, a) = log prior(q, a) + βᵀe(q, a) + zᵢᵀWe(q, a)

e is the 64-feature question-answer representation; β and W are shared weights; zᵢ is the person’s eight-number vector. The prior pools smoothed training answer counts for questions with exactly matching option labels and order. An unseen scale receives a uniform prior.

Qwen remains frozen. The coordinates are learned factors with no assigned psychological labels.

Development results

  • Larger nonlinear models improved training fit but performed worse on validation.
  • The selected linear model added a training-derived population prior and stronger regularisation.
  • The population baseline remained slightly better overall on validation.
Selected development comparisons. Same validation set: 300 people × eight questions.
ApproachTraining accuracyValidation accuracyValidation log loss ↓
Original linear model51.6%34.3%1.576
Larger nonlinear model63.4%25.4%2.975
Prior + regularised linear model55.4%36.0%1.515
Population baselinen/a36.6%1.513

Baseline: pooled training answer frequencies for identical ordered option labels. Selection used validation log loss.

Respondent-vector checks

  • Correct vectors outperformed shuffled vectors, indicating person-specific predictive information.
  • A common mean vector still performed slightly better overall on validation.
  • Shuffling leaves group shares unchanged; aggregate fit alone cannot establish individual accuracy.

PredictorExact-answer accuracyLog loss ↓
100 personas46.3%1.301
Population baseline32.3%1.431

  • 139 of 300 answers predicted correctly, compared with 97 for the population baseline.
  • 95% respondent-bootstrap interval for the accuracy gain: +7.3 to +20.7 percentage points. Conditional on these three questions; question and model-selection uncertainty excluded.

Group support estimates

  • Mean support-share error: personas 7.0 pp; population baseline 7.0 pp; shared model only 2.6 pp.
  • Full-distribution error: mean total variation 14.9% for personas and 14.6% for the population baseline.
  • Finding: improved individual prediction on these items, with no improvement in aggregate calibration.

New survey and simulation

  • Five allocations rated independently on the same single-select scale.
  • Only the budget split changes. Ratings measure support; they do not identify an exclusive preferred package.

The exact scenario

Consider a hypothetical federal program for 2027 with a fixed total budget of $1 billion, including delivery costs, to help low-income U.S. households with home energy costs. The money has already been set aside; choosing a package does not change total spending or taxes. Bill credits reduce recipients' electricity or heating bills during 2027. Home energy improvements, such as insulation and efficient heating equipment, are intended to reduce bills in later years. Both renters and homeowners can qualify; support for rental properties must benefit the tenant. The five packages are alternatives, and only one would be implemented. Evaluate each package independently.

Would you support or oppose…

Q1Allocating 100% of the program budget to immediate bill credits and 0% to home energy improvements?
Q2Allocating 75% of the program budget to immediate bill credits and 25% to home energy improvements?
Q3Allocating 50% of the program budget to immediate bill credits and 50% to home energy improvements?
Q4Allocating 25% of the program budget to immediate bill credits and 75% to home energy improvements?
Q5Allocating 0% of the program budget to immediate bill credits and 100% to home energy improvements?

Choose one answer for each question:

  1. Strongly oppose
  2. Somewhat oppose
  3. Neither oppose nor support
  4. Somewhat support
  5. Strongly support

  • Decision implication: no supported allocation recommendation; human testing is required.

Technical details

  • Selected checkpoint: prior_linear_l2_01; 64 whitened PCA features; eight respondent coordinates.
  • Parameters: 576 shared weights; 13,840 including background vectors; 800 additional coordinates for the final personas.
  • Persona fitting: initialised at the mean background vector; Adam, 200 steps, learning rate 0.03, L2 0.1.
  • Question bank: 441 items and 1,877 options. PCA fitted on 1,822 training-option embeddings.

Sources

  1. Toubia et al., Twin-2K-500 (2025)

    Dataset and linked person-level ground truth. This experiment uses its own split and evaluation.

  2. Park et al., self-report grounded agents (2026 revision)

    Grounding in actual interviews and survey self-reports.

  3. Suh et al., SubPOP (ACL 2025)

    Fine-tuning to predict subpopulation response distributions, rather than individual twins.

  4. Hu et al., LoRA (2021)

    An efficient adaptation technique, not a guarantee of survey accuracy.

  5. Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B model card

    Official model card for the frozen encoder used here.

  6. Krsteski et al., survey simulation and rectification (ACL 2026)

    Using human data to correct bias in population estimates; not implemented here.

  7. Williams et al., Beyond Marginal Distributions (ACL Findings 2026)

    Evaluating joint response patterns as well as marginal distributions.
